findings.scenario: Reviewer: run two daemons with `tc qdisc add dev lo root netem delay 50ms` (100 ms RTT) on a 1 Gbps link and publish a 500 MB PSD. The TXFR stream is bounded by the receiver's default stream_receive_window of 1,250,000 B: throughput <= 1.25 MB / 0.1 s = 12.5 MB/s (100 Mbps), so the file takes ~40 s instead of ~5 s; a 100 GB checkpoint takes ~2.2 h instead of ~15 min. `transfer list` speed plateaus at ~100 Mbps on every path with >= 100 ms RTT regardless of link capacity. With 50 files in parallel the connection-level send_window (10 MB) caps the whole connection at 100 MB/s at 100 ms. Memory is unbounded in the other direction: receive_window is VarInt::MAX.
findings.impact_ai_game: Cross-site studios (Tokyo/Osaka/overseas outsourcers), remote artists on 30-100 ms paths and cloud GPU nodes pulling checkpoints are all BDP-bound; the link is mostly idle while artists wait. The DESIGN promise of bandwidth-aware classes cannot work when the per-stream window silently caps every class.
findings.current_state: Both ClientConfig and ServerConfig set only max_concurrent_bidi_streams and max_idle_timeout; every other quinn knob is at the 0.11.17 default (Cubic, initial_mtu 1200 with DPLPMTUD to 1452, GSO on, keep_alive None, ack_frequency None, stream window 1.25 MB, send_window 10 MB, receive_window unbounded). `max_udp_payload_size` and `enable_0rtt` are parsed but never applied.
findings.proposed_redesign: Add an explicit transport profile in QuicConfig and apply it in build_client_config_for/build_server_config: stream_receive_window = clamp(target_bw * max_rtt, 1.25 MiB, 32 MiB) (default 16 MiB), send_window = 4 x stream window (64 MiB), receive_window = min(max_concurrent_streams x stream window, 256 MiB) to bound receiver memory, datagram buffers unchanged, keep MTU discovery on with initial_mtu 1200 (tunnels/VPN), keep Cubic as default and expose BBR behind `congestion = "bbr"` (experimental), optional ack_frequency_config for >1 Gbps paths. Derive the live BDP from quinn::Connection::stats().path.rtt and delivered bytes to pick the lan/wan profile per peer. Delete or implement the dead knobs (max_udp_payload_size -> transport.initial_mtu/min_mtu; enable_0rtt -> remove until a replay-safe stream class exists). Validate in NetConfig::validate that window >= 2 x CHUNK_SIZE and <= memory budget.
alternatives: Spread a file across N parallel streams (needed anyway, TRN-WP-03/04): N x 1.25 MB in flight, but the connection send_window (10 MB) still caps at 100 MB/s at 100 ms RTT unless raised
Several QUIC connections per peer as DESIGN 15.3 max_connections suggests: more complex registry, same window problem per connection
Kernel TCP/TLS for intra-datacenter bulk moves where QUIC's per-core cost dominates (research: kernel TCP up to 3x best QUIC stack)

findings.scenario: Reviewer: send a 100 GB checkpoint over 10 GbE loopback. The sender issues 1.6 M frames, each costing one blocking file read, one 64 KiB BLAKE3, two 64 KiB memcpys (to_vec, msgpack encode) and two write_all calls; the receiver allocates a Vec per frame, decodes (copy), hashes, then awaits an unbuffered tokio File write before reading the next frame, so network receive and disk write never overlap. Per the research, a single QUIC connection on one core sustains roughly 0.5-1.5 Gbps even with GSO, so the 100 GB transfer takes 9-27 min where the line allows 80 s; on 1 GbE the pipeline is line-bound (13.3 min) but a slow receiver disk (HDD/NAS 150 MB/s) directly throttles the stream because the write is inline.
findings.impact_ai_game: Checkpoint and dataset movement inside a studio LAN/cluster is CPU-bound far below 10 GbE; large FBX/PSD sets are serialized through one stream each, so a single slow receiver disk or hash thread sets the pace for the whole file.
findings.current_state: Fixed 64 KiB msgpack frames with serde-encoded hashes, one bidi stream per file, sequential loops on both ends, no read-ahead or write-behind, no size-class chunking, no Bytes/zero-copy; MAX_FRAME = 66560.
findings.proposed_redesign: Replace the frame format with a fixed binary header (magic, version, flags, u64 offset, u32 len) and payload passed as bytes::Bytes from a pooled buffer into quinn::SendStream::write_chunk (zero copy); frame size by class (1 MiB Large, 256 KiB Medium, 64 KiB Small) as DESIGN 15.2 specifies; sender pipeline = disk reader task (read-ahead 4-8 frames, 1-4 MiB reads) -> bounded channel -> stream writer; receiver pipeline = stream reader -> bounded channel -> verifier/writer with >= 1 MiB coalesced writes (BufWriter or direct), hashing in the verifier task; split a file into N range-partitioned streams (N from class and measured BDP) so one slow stream does not stall the file; use rayon/multithreaded BLAKE3 for the tree hash (TRN-WP-08).
alternatives: Only enlarge CHUNK_SIZE (cuts per-frame overhead but keeps the sequential loop and single stream)

findings.scenario: Reviewer: start a 100 GB checkpoint pull over a 100 Mbps link (2.2 h) and drop the connection at 95 % (Wi-Fi roam, VPN rekey, laptop sleep, publisher daemon restart). The receiver deletes incoming-<uuid>.part, the ActiveTransfer becomes Failed, nothing retries; the user re-issues the want and pays another 2.2 h. Three history nodes that all hold the version cannot share the load: handle_file_want on whichever node answers first pushes the whole file alone, and the fastest node is not chosen (bandwidth estimate is always 0, TRN-WP-11).
findings.impact_ai_game: Multi-GB checkpoints, datasets and cinematic assets over WAN are exactly the transfers that get interrupted; per-range verification and multi-source striping are what Kraken/Dragonfly/BitTorrent/Storj use to make such transfers finish predictably (p99 18 s for 3 GB to 2,600 hosts in Kraken).
findings.current_state: Push-only whole-file protocol; header has no range; failure path unlinks the partial file; one source per transfer; the IPFS-style multi-source design in DESIGN 15.1 exists only as dormant catalog-block bitswap code.
findings.proposed_redesign: Content-addressed range pull protocol: receiver opens a TXFR stream with WANT { project, path, version, blake3, ranges[] } and the holder replies with verified range frames; keep the .part file plus a verified-range bitmap (persisted next to it) so resume requests only missing ranges; verify every range against the whole-file BLAKE3 using a Bao outboard tree (16 KiB groups, ~0.4 % overhead) shipped once per file, so a corrupt range from one source aborts that source only; stripe disjoint ranges across all peers that announced the hash (history nodes first), re-issue slow ranges to another source near the end (endgame/hedged requests); sweep stale .part files by age. Offers carry the hash so receivers can pull from any holder, not only the publisher.
alternatives: tus-style offset resume without per-range verification (simpler; a corrupt tail forces full re-download; no multi-source)
Erasure coding across history nodes (Storj k/n) — overhead unjustified for 3-10 nodes; range striping with hedging gives the same tail-latency benefit

findings.scenario: Reviewer: enable history on the publisher and publish a 100 GB checkpoint from NVMe (2 GB/s read, 1.5 GB/s write; BLAKE3 ~1.5 GB/s single thread). Before the FileOffer is gossiped the daemon performs CRC (50 s) + copy (50 s read + 67 s write) + CRC of the copy (50 s) + BLAKE3 of the copy (67 s) = ~4.7 min, during which the QUIC connection idles out (TRN-WP-02). Then each FileWant triggers hash_file again (67 s) before execute_send opens the stream, so with five requesters the publisher reads 500 GB and hashes 500 GB for one publish, and every requester waits >1 min for the first byte. On an HDD/NAS depot (150 MB/s) the same publish costs ~55 min plus 11 min per requester. Without history the publish still costs 3 full reads (CRC, hash_file, send).
findings.impact_ai_game: Time-to-first-byte for checkpoints and big scenes is dominated by local re-reads, not the network; per-requester rehashing makes fan-out to a render farm/cluster O(N x file size) on the publisher's disk.

findings.scenario: Reviewer: publish 1,024 files (MAX_PATHS_PER_PUBLISH) to 5 peers. The publisher opens 5,120 Offer streams + 5 CatalogUpdate streams; each receiver's gossip handler delivers into a tokio broadcast channel of capacity 256 while its subscriber is busy spawning fetch_file tasks, so Lagged(n) fires and the dropped offers are never pulled until that path is republished; each receiver then broadcasts 1,024 Want streams to all 5 peers (5,120 more), every peer fetches the catalog block over bitswap and discards it, and the publisher spawns 1,024 hash_file + TXFR tasks. Per-file latency floor = Offer (0.5 RTT) + Want (0.5 RTT) + open_bi/header (0.5 RTT) + publisher hash time; the receiving GUI shows 0 % until the file completes.

alternatives: Keep gossipsub semantics but implement IHAVE/IWANT batching and a proper mesh so fan-out is not all-connections
Increase channel capacity (hides the burst problem until the next size)
